ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries taste, sensation, and parasympathetic fibers from the tongue, pharynx, and carotid body. It links the brainstem to key reflexes for swallowing and blood pressure control.

sections.p: CN IX emerges from the medulla, exits the skull through the jugular foramen, and supplies the posterior tongue, pharynx, middle ear, and carotid sinus.
b: Key for gag reflex and baroreceptor signaling

sections.p: The nerve has a rootlet in the nucleus ambiguus and solitary nucleus, then travels laterally with the vagus before exiting the skull.
b: Rootlets join to form a single trunk
Divides into tympanic, carotid, and pharyngeal branches

sections.p: Within the jugular foramen it lies medial to the vagus and lateral to the accessory nerve, and runs alongside the internal carotid artery.
b: Close to cranial nerves X and XI
Adjacent to the internal jugular vein

sections.p: Supplied by branches of the ascending pharyngeal artery and small branches from the occipital artery.
b: Vascular supply mirrors nearby pharyngeal arteries

sections.p: Provides afferent taste from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue, general sensation from the oropharynx, and efferent parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland.
b: Taste via chorda tympani joins only for anterior tongue

sections.p: Mediates taste, gag reflex, swallowing coordination, and baroreceptor reflexes that regulate blood pressure.
b: Detects blood oxygen and pressure via carotid body

sections.p: Lesions cause loss of taste, impaired gag reflex, dysphagia, and abnormal blood pressure responses. Common causes include skull base tumors, jugular foramen syndrome, and infections such as TB meningitis.
b: Absent gag reflex on the affected side
Unstable heart rate with positional changes

t.a: MRI of brainstem and skull base
t.b: Identifies compressive lesions; if unavailable, use CT with contrast
Assesses baroreceptor function; a blunted response suggests glossopharyngeal involvement
Detects dysphagia severity; if unavailable, bedside swallow assessment is used

sections.p: Test taste on posterior third of tongue, assess gag reflex, and check for orthostatic hypotension to infer carotid sinus involvement.
b: Blood pressure: measure supine and standing

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of gag reflex leading to aspiration pneumonia

faq.q: Why does a glossopharyngeal lesion affect blood pressure?
faq.a: The nerve carries afferents from the carotid sinus; damage disrupts baroreceptor signaling, causing unstable BP.

faq.q: Can a stroke affect CN IX alone?
faq.a: Isolated lesions are rare; most strokes involve adjacent nuclei, but a small lateral medullary infarct can spare other cranial nerves.

faq.q: What distinguishes glossopharyngeal from vagus nerve deficits?
faq.a: CN IX loss affects posterior tongue taste and carotid sinus; CN X loss adds voice changes and loss of cough reflex.

exam: Explain how loss of the gag reflex points to glossopharyngeal nerve injury.
Describe the pathway by which the glossopharyngeal nerve contributes to blood pressure regulation.
List the key clinical tests to evaluate glossopharyngeal function.
